name: Inversion method / scalp stretching exercises

lead: Some hair-loss communities hang upside down or stretch and massage the scalp, hoping for thicker hair. The idea is that a looser scalp and more blood flow to it supports regrowth, and followers use it as a drug-free option.

The proposed chain is more scalp circulation or less scalp tightness, then hair growth. Inversion therapy is otherwise a form of spinal traction, and no published studies of either practice for hair growth were found.

paras: People hang from inversion tables or gravity boots for short sessions, or do manual scalp massage and stretching as a daily routine. It is usually done alongside other hair-loss approaches, and followers describe it as an ongoing habit rather than a short course.
Inversion raises heart rate and venous return and is listed as higher-risk for people with heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma, reflux or pregnancy. Scalp massage is generally low-risk.

web.title: Koyama et al. 2016, Standardized scalp massage (ePlasty)

angle.text: Some hair-loss communities hang upside down or stretch the scalp, believing a looser scalp and better blood flow supports thicker regrowth. Inversion is a spinal-traction technique, and no hair studies of these practices have been published.

lead: Inversion methods and scalp stretching exercises are drug-free routines that hair-loss and appearance communities use in the hope of keeping or thickening scalp hair. One strand involves hanging inverted on an inversion table or in gravity boots so that blood flows toward the head; the other involves manually massaging or stretching the scalp over the skull to loosen it and, proponents say, improve circulation to the follicles.

Inversion therapy itself is a form of spinal traction in which a person hangs by the legs, ankles or feet at an angle or fully upside down.[1] Gravity boots, usually hung from a doorway or pull-up bar, and inversion tables that tilt the user are the two common devices.[1] Scalp massage, by contrast, can be done by hand or with a handheld massager and takes a few minutes a day.

Published research exists for scalp massage but not for inversion. A 2016 study by Koyama and colleagues in ePlasty followed nine healthy men using a scalp massage device for four minutes a day for 24 weeks, and also stretched cultured dermal papilla cells in the lab, reporting changes in hair-cycle-related gene expression.[2] No clinical study of hanging upside down for hair growth has been found.

paras: Proponents describe two related practices: spending time inverted so blood flows toward the head, and moving or stretching the scalp over the skull to reduce a perceived tightness. Neither is a recognised medical treatment for hair loss.

Inversion therapy means hanging at an inverted angle, usually with gravity boots or an inversion table, and is a form of spinal traction.[1] Its stated theory is that gravity-assisted traction temporarily increases spacing between vertebrae, which may ease pressure on nerve roots and relax muscles.[1] Encyclopedic sources describe the usual benefit as feeling pleasant during the session.[1]

The inverted position raises heart rate, cardiac output, peripheral resistance, venous return and myocardial oxygen consumption.[1] People with heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma or other eye disease, or pregnancy are listed as being at higher risk, acid reflux combined with inversion can be painful and nauseating, and sessions of about 10 minutes at most are mentioned.[1]

In the 2016 ePlasty study, nine healthy Japanese men aged 25 to 46 without obvious hair loss used a Panasonic scalp massage device for four minutes a day for 24 weeks on one temporal area, with the other side as an untreated control.[2] Hair thickness in the massaged area rose from 0.085 to 0.092 mm, and the authors concluded that standardized massage increased hair thickness.[2]

The paper also reports that hair density in the massaged area fell at 12 weeks, which the authors suggested could reflect temporary shedding of resting-phase hairs, and that figure captions show no significant difference between massaged and control sides, with the timing of the thickness increase described inconsistently.[2] In the lab part, human dermal papilla cells stretched for 72 hours showed higher expression of BMP4, NOGGIN, SMAD4 and IL6ST and lower expression of IL6, and modelling indicated massage produces displacement and stress in subcutaneous tissue.[2] The authors note the small sample, partial funding by a company, and that blood flow and tissue biopsies were not evaluated.[2]
One small human study of daily scalp massage over 24 weeks, described above, reported increased hair thickness in healthy men.[2] No studies found on inversion or gravity boots for hair growth.

lore.intro: The methods circulate in hair-loss forums and fringe appearance content as no-drug options, with scalp massage generally treated as gentle and inversion as the more extreme version.

claims.claim: Hanging upside down increases scalp blood flow and regrows hair

timeline.event: Koyama and colleagues publish a 24-week scalp massage study in nine men together with dermal papilla cell stretching experiments.[2]
